questions.question_text: Which of the following is a factor of $P(x)=x^3-7x+6$?

options.why: $P(-1)=-1+7+6=12\neq 0$, so $(x+1)$ does not divide evenly.
$P(3)=27-21+6=12\neq 0$, so $(x-3)$ leaves a remainder.
$P(-2)=-8+14+6=12\neq 0$; the factor is $(x-2)$, from the zero $x=2$.
The divisor $(x+4)$ is zero at $x=-4$, so factorhood is decided by $P(-4)$, not $P(4)$.
$P(4)=144\neq 0$; the correct test for $(x+4)$ is $P(-4)$, which does equal $0$.
A sign slip evaluating $5(-4)^2$ as $-80$ gives $-160$; correctly, $P(-4)=-64+80-8-8=0$.

questions.question_text: $(x+2)$ is a factor of $P(x)=x^3+kx^2-5x+6$. Find the value of $k$.

options.why: A sign error isolating $k$ from $4k+8=0$; dividing by $4$ gives $k=-2$.
Evaluating at $x=2$ instead of $x=-2$ sets up $4k+4=0$, giving $-1$.
Evaluating $-5(-2)$ as $-10$ instead of $+10$ sets up $4k-12=0$, giving $3$.
The zeros' signs are flipped: a factor $(x+4)$ gives the zero $x=-4$, not $x=4$.
The factor $(x-3)$ gives the zero $x=3$; only factors of the form $(x+a)$ give negative zeros.
These multiply to give the constant $-12$, but none of them is actually a zero of the polynomial.

questions.question_text: $P(x)$ divided by $(x-5)$ leaves remainder $0$. Which statement must be true?

options.why: The divisor $(x-5)$ is zero at $x=5$, so the zero is $5$, not $-5$.
The remainder theorem gives $P(5)=0$ here, not $5$; the remainder is the value of $P(5)$.

options.text: The quotient of the division is zero
options.why: A zero remainder means the division is exact; the quotient is generally a nonzero polynomial.

questions.solution_text:
Remainder $0$ means $P(5)=0$.
By the factor theorem, $(x-5)$ is a factor of $P(x)$.

questions.question_text: According to the integer root theorem, which list contains all possible integer zeroes of $P(x)=x^3+4x^2+x+10$?

options.why: Negative factors of the constant term are also candidates — a zero can be negative.
These are factors of the coefficient $4$; candidates come from the constant term $10$.
Every factor of $10$ is a candidate, not just $10$ itself: $\pm 1,\ \pm 2,\ \pm 5$ must also be tested.

questions.solution_text:
All coefficients are integers, so any integer zero must be a factor of the constant term $10$.
Candidates: $\pm 1,\ \pm 2,\ \pm 5,\ \pm 10$

questions.question_text: $(3x+1)$ is a factor of $P(x)$ if which condition holds?

options.why: $3x+1=0$ at $x=-\frac{1}{3}$; the positive value matches the divisor $(3x-1)$ instead.
This inverts the fraction: solve $3x+1=0$ to get $x=-\frac{1}{3}$, not $x=-3$.
Neither the sign nor the value is right; substitute the zero of the divisor, $x=-\frac{1}{3}$.

questions.solution_text:
$3x+1=0$ when $x=-\frac{1}{3}$
$(3x+1)$ is a factor of $P(x)$ if $P\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)=0$.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum number of zeroes a polynomial of degree $5$ can have?

options.why: Subtracting one from the degree counts maximum turning points, not zeroes.
A degree-$5$ polynomial has at most $5$ linear factors, so at most $5$ zeroes.
The degree caps the number of linear factors, so the count of zeroes is bounded by the degree.

questions.solution_text:
A polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ zeroes.
Maximum number of zeroes: $5$

questions.question_text: By testing factors of the constant term, find a factor of $P(x)=x^3+3x^2+7x+5$.

options.why: $P(1)=1+3+7+5=16\neq 0$, so $(x-1)$ is not a factor.
